title: Introduction to the Epistles of Peter
subtitle: A concise guide to the authorship, setting, readers, and purposes of the two letters Simon Peter sent to believers in Asia Minor.

blocks.text: Both letters open with the name of Peter. The first introduces its writer as an apostle of Jesus Christ, and later as a fellow elder who witnessed the sufferings of Christ. The second uses the fuller Hebrew form Simeon Peter and calls its writer a servant as well as an apostle. These are not passing labels. Each letter speaks with the settled authority of someone who walked with Jesus, who expects to be heard by churches across a wide region, and who writes as a shepherd who has himself been restored after failure.

The earliest Christian writers treated 1 Peter as the apostle’s own work. Its language echoes in a letter sent from the church at Rome near the end of the first century, Polycarp of Smyrna draws on it freely, and by the late second century it is cited by name across the Christian world. Later objections usually rest on four points: the Greek is polished, the thought resembles Paul, the letter tells few stories from the life of Jesus, and Peter had no known link with the churches of Asia Minor. None of these settles the matter. The letter itself says it was written through Silvanus, a trusted companion who may well have shaped the wording. Shared themes with Paul reflect a common apostolic gospel, and the writer’s memories of Jesus run beneath the surface in phrases about tending the flock, being clothed with humility, and following in the steps of the suffering Servant.

The second letter has a harder history. It was slower to gain universal acceptance, and some leaders in the third and fourth centuries voiced doubts about it, largely because its style differs from 1 Peter and because it circulated less widely at first. Modern readers raise further questions about its close agreement with the letter of Jude, its reference to a collection of Paul’s letters, and its resemblance to a farewell testament. These questions deserve a fair hearing, yet none of them requires a later author writing under Peter’s name.

Several considerations favor apostolic authorship. The letter makes repeated personal claims: the writer saw the transfiguration on the holy mountain, heard the voice from the majestic glory, knows that the Lord has shown him his death is near, and refers back to a previous letter to the same readers. The early church consistently rejected writings known to be falsely attributed, so the eventual recognition of 2 Peter suggests that its readers were persuaded it came from the apostle. Differences of style are natural if Peter wrote this letter with a different helper, or with less help, and on a more urgent subject. Its use of material shared with Jude fits a time when church leaders faced the same dangers and drew on common warnings. This study therefore reads both letters as the authentic voice of Simon Peter.

First Peter closes with greetings from the church in Babylon. The ancient city on the Euphrates had dwindled by this time, and there is no early memory of Peter working there. Babylon had become a familiar way of speaking about Rome, the imperial capital that held God’s people far from their true home, much as the empire of Nebuchadnezzar once held Judah in exile. The name completes a picture that begins in the letter’s first line, where the readers are called exiles of the dispersion. Early Christian memory also places Peter in Rome in his final years, along with Mark, whom the letter mentions in the same closing greeting.

Paul’s letters written from Rome do not mention Peter, which suggests that the apostle arrived there late, perhaps near the time of Paul’s final imprisonment. The hostility described in 1 Peter, where believers are slandered as evildoers and warned of a fiery trial, fits the tense atmosphere of the early sixties, around the time when Nero turned public blame for the great fire of A.D. 64 against the Christians of the city. A date around A.D. 63 to 65 is therefore reasonable for the first letter, though certainty is not possible.

Second Peter was written shortly before the apostle’s death, which early tradition places in Rome during Nero’s reign, probably no later than about A.D. 67 or 68. The letter does not name its place of writing, but Rome remains the most natural setting. Peter writes knowing that he must soon put off the tent of his body, and he wants his readers to remember these things after his departure. The two letters therefore come from the closing stage of his ministry, separated by only a few years.

First Peter is addressed to believers scattered across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. Together these regions covered most of the land north of the Taurus Mountains in what is now Turkey, an area of busy coastal cities, Roman colonies, and wide rural highlands. The order of the names may trace the route of a messenger who landed on the Black Sea coast, traveled through the interior, and returned to the north. The letter was meant to be carried from congregation to congregation and read aloud in each one.

Most of the readers appear to have been Gentiles. Peter reminds them that they once lived in ignorance, that they were formerly not a people, and that their old companions are surprised when they no longer join in drunken feasts and idolatrous worship. Yet Jewish believers were present as well, and the letter is saturated with the language of Israel’s Scriptures. Peter applies to the whole church the titles once given to Israel at Sinai: an elect people, a priesthood serving the King, a nation set apart, and God’s own possession. The apostle who first opened the door of the church to Gentiles now addresses Jew and Gentile together as one household of faith.

Peter calls his readers strangers and sojourners. Some of them may have been literal outsiders, people without full civic standing, migrants, or residents of colonies settled from elsewhere. All of them had become outsiders in a deeper sense through conversion. Their new allegiance to Christ separated them from family religion, civic festivals, and trade associations that ordinary life assumed. The letter includes household slaves, wives married to unbelieving husbands, husbands, elders, and younger members, showing that the gospel had reached people at every level of the household.

Second Peter addresses those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with the apostles and refers to itself as a second letter to the same readers. It is most natural, then, to see the same churches of Asia Minor in view. Their immediate danger had shifted. Pressure from outside had not disappeared, but teachers from within were now offering a version of Christian freedom that loosened moral restraint and ridiculed the promise of Christ’s return.

Simon was a fisherman from Bethsaida who lived in Capernaum by the Sea of Galilee, working alongside his brother Andrew and in partnership with James and John. Jesus called him from his nets and gave him the name Cephas, or Peter, meaning rock. He became the leading voice among the Twelve, confessing Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, witnessing the transfiguration, and walking on the water before his faith faltered. On the night of the betrayal he denied his Lord three times, and after the resurrection Jesus restored him beside the lake with a threefold commission to feed His sheep.

At Pentecost Peter preached the risen Christ in Jerusalem, and thousands were baptized. He healed in the name of Jesus, stood before the council, endured prison and beatings, and opened the gospel to the Gentile household of Cornelius after God showed him that no person should be called common or unclean. When Herod Agrippa imprisoned him, an angel led him out, and he went to another place. Paul later named him among the pillars of the Jerusalem church and recognized his special calling to the circumcision, while also confronting him at Antioch when he withdrew from Gentile believers.

blocks.title: Milestones in Peter’s Life
blocks.note: Dates are approximate, and the details of Peter’s later travels are known only in outline.

events.title: Called from the Nets
events.description: Jesus calls Simon and Andrew by the Sea of Galilee and names Simon Cephas, the rock.

events.title: Denial and Restoration
events.description: Peter denies Jesus three times, then meets the risen Lord, who recommissions him to feed His sheep.

events.title: Preaching at Pentecost
events.description: Peter proclaims the crucified and risen Christ in Jerusalem, and about three thousand are baptized.

events.title: The Door Opened to Gentiles
events.description: At Caesarea Peter preaches to Cornelius and his household, who receive the Spirit and are baptized.

events.title: Prison and the Jerusalem Council
events.description: Delivered from Herod’s prison, Peter later defends the inclusion of Gentiles by grace at the council in Jerusalem.

events.title: 1 Peter from Babylon
events.description: From Rome Peter writes through Silvanus to strengthen suffering believers across Asia Minor.

events.title: 2 Peter and Martyrdom
events.description: Near death, Peter writes his final letter and is martyred in Rome under Nero, as Jesus had foretold.

blocks.text: The later years of Peter’s ministry are known only in part. He traveled with his wife in the work of the gospel, believers in Corinth knew his name, and he appears to have spent his final period in Rome with Mark and Silvanus at his side. Jesus had told him that when he was old another would bind him and lead him where he did not wish to go. The two letters reflect that whole life: the impulsive disciple has become a patient shepherd, the man who once refused the cross now calls believers to follow the suffering Christ, and the one who fell now warns others to stand firm.

sections.title: Suffering and Hope in the Roman World

blocks.text: The suffering described in 1 Peter was mainly social before it became official. Neighbors spoke against believers as evildoers, mocked their refusal to share in former pleasures, and treated them as disloyal to family and city. In the Roman world religion was bound up with household gods, civic festivals, guild banquets, and honor paid to the emperor. Someone who withdrew from these practices could be seen as rude, antisocial, or even dangerous to the peace that the gods were thought to protect. Slaves with harsh masters and wives with unbelieving husbands felt this pressure inside their own homes.

Peter also warns of a fiery trial already beginning. Suffering for the name of Christ was becoming a recognized possibility, and the mention of being reproached as a Christian shows that the label itself could bring shame. There is no need to imagine an empire-wide legal campaign at this stage. Local hostility, informal accusations, and occasional action by magistrates were enough to make discipleship costly. The cruelty Nero unleashed on believers in Rome soon afterward showed how quickly such hostility could turn deadly, and Peter writes as one who would share that end.

Against this background the letter grounds endurance in hope. Believers have been born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, to an inheritance kept in heaven and ready to be revealed in the last time. Present trials are brief and refining, like fire testing gold. Christ’s own suffering is both the means of redemption and the pattern for His followers, who entrust themselves to the faithful Creator by doing good. Behind human opposition Peter sees a deeper conflict with the adversary who prowls like a roaring lion, and he assures the church that the God of all grace will restore, establish, and strengthen them after they have suffered a little while.

Peter wrote first to remind scattered believers of who they are. Their identity rests on the work of the Father, the Spirit, and the Son: they are chosen in keeping with the foreknowledge of God the Father, set apart by the Spirit, and called to obedience and cleansing through the blood of Jesus. That calling does not depend on social approval. People rejected by their neighbors are living stones being built into a spiritual house, a priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Christ.

A second aim was to show how such people should live among those who misunderstand them. Peter urges them to keep their conduct honorable so that slander will be silenced and some observers may glorify God. He gives instruction for relations with civil authority, for household servants, for wives and husbands, and for the whole congregation. Submission in these settings is never surrender of conscience. It is a deliberate witness, shaped by the example of Christ, who did not return insult for insult and entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly.

Peter also wanted to prepare the church for suffering without fear or surprise. He reminds them that suffering for righteousness carries a blessing that suffering for wrongdoing never can, that Christ suffered once for sins to bring us to God, and that baptism saves as the pledge of a good conscience toward God through the resurrection. As in the days of Noah, a small company is preserved while the world disregards God’s patience. The end of all things is near, so believers are to be sober, to pray, to love earnestly, and to use every gift as stewards of God’s varied grace.

Finally, the letter strengthens leadership and unity. Elders are to shepherd the flock willingly and by example, looking to the Chief Shepherd who will appear. Younger members are to be humble, and all are to cast their anxieties on God. Peter sums up his purpose in a single line near the end: he has written briefly to encourage them and to testify that this is the true grace of God, in which they are to stand.

Second Peter is the apostle’s final appeal. He knows that his death is near, and he wants to leave the churches a lasting reminder of what they have already received. God’s divine power has granted everything needed for life and godliness through the knowledge of Christ, and believers have been given precious promises so that they may share in the divine nature and escape the corruption of the world. Peter urges them to add to their faith virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection, and love, and so to make their calling and election sure.

The letter answers a serious threat from within. False teachers were rising among the believers, bringing in destructive heresies, denying the Master who bought them, and exploiting others through greed and sensual freedom. They promised liberty while they themselves were slaves of corruption. Peter recalls the fallen angels, the world of Noah’s day, and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, which were reduced to ashes, to show that God knows how to rescue the godly and to keep the unrighteous under guard until the day of judgment.

Peter also defends the certainty of Christ’s return. Scoffers argued that nothing had changed since the fathers fell asleep and that the promise of His coming had failed. Peter answers that the same word which formed the world and later flooded it is reserving the present heavens and earth for fire. With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and His apparent delay is patience, because He is not willing that any should perish. The day of the Lord will come as a thief, sin will be destroyed, and God’s people look for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.

Throughout, Peter roots this hope in trustworthy testimony. He and the other apostles did not follow cleverly devised myths; they were eyewitnesses of Christ’s majesty on the holy mountain. The prophetic word is made even more sure, a lamp shining in a dark place, because no prophecy came by human will. Holy men of God spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. The letter ends with a call to grow in grace and in the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

The two letters address the same churches at different moments of danger. First Peter speaks to believers pressed from outside by slander, social exclusion, and the threat of open persecution. Second Peter speaks to the same communities when the gravest danger has moved inside the congregations, where corrupt teachers deny the moral claims of the gospel and the promise of the Lord’s return. One letter teaches the church how to suffer faithfully; the other teaches it how to remain faithful when error presents itself as freedom.

Both letters look steadily toward the appearing of Jesus Christ. First Peter speaks of a salvation ready to be revealed, of grace brought at the revelation of Jesus, and of a crown of glory given when the Chief Shepherd appears. Second Peter defends the same coming against mockery and describes its cosmic scope. In each case hope for the future produces holiness in the present. Believers are to be sober, watchful, loving, and diligent, living as people who belong to the coming kingdom while still among the nations.

Read together, the letters reveal a pastor whose own story has been shaped by grace. The man who once tried to turn Jesus away from suffering now calls believers to follow Him through it, and the disciple who once fell now urges them to stand firm and grow. Both letters rest on the prophetic Scriptures, the apostolic witness to Christ, and the faithfulness of God, who keeps His people through faith until the last day.

blocks.title: Book at a Glance
rows: Author
Simon Peter, apostle of Jesus Christ, writing the first letter through Silvanus
Dates
1 Peter: about A.D. 63–65; 2 Peter: shortly before Peter’s death, about A.D. 66–68
Place of writing
Rome, called Babylon in the greeting of the first letter
Original readers
Mostly Gentile congregations, with Jewish believers among them, in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia
Setting
Social hostility and growing persecution from outside, followed by false teaching and scoffing from within
1 Peter
Encourages exiles to stand in the true grace of God, to live honorably among unbelievers, and to suffer as Christ suffered
2 Peter
Calls believers to grow in godliness, warns against false teachers, and affirms the certainty of Christ’s return
Central message
Those born again to a living hope through the risen Christ are kept by God’s power for His coming and are called to holy living now
Representative passages

blocks.title: The Two Letters Compared
rows: Main danger
Slander, exclusion, and persecution from unbelieving neighbors
False teachers inside the church and scoffers mocking the promise
Primary call
Endure suffering with good conduct and steady hope
Grow in grace and knowledge and guard against error
View of the future
A salvation and inheritance ready to be revealed when Christ appears
The day of the Lord, the cleansing fire, and new heavens and a new earth
Use of Scripture
Frequent direct quotation of the prophets, Psalms, and Proverbs
Appeal to the sure prophetic word and to examples of judgment and rescue
Pastoral tone
Tender encouragement for exiles under pressure
Urgent farewell from an apostle facing death
